content.text: {"relation":"NOVEL","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the visionary 'living creatures' of Ezekiel 1/10 and Revelation 4-5: exalted angelic throne attendants identified with the cherubim, symbolically representing the whole of animate creation in worship (with the four-Evangelists/tetramorph reading as the major traditional alternative, plus Christ-attributes, tribal-standard, zodiacal, and the plain lexical Genesis sense as secondary options).","book_summary":"The book defines 'living creature' as a nation or organized people — the living, positive counterpart of a 'beast' (which in prophetic symbolism denotes a kingdom or ruler). Its proof-texts are Daniel 7:3,17 (beasts = kings/kingdoms) and the sea-judgment passages Revelation 8:9 and 16:3 (creatures in the sea that have life and die), not the throne visions of Ezekiel 1 or Revelation 4.","consensus_core_identification":"Living creatures = cherubim-class angelic beings attending God's throne, symbolizing all animate creation (or, traditionally, the four Evangelists) in the throne visions of Ezekiel and Revelation.","book_core_identification":"Living creature = a nation or organized body of people, the living analogue of the symbolic 'beast' (kingdom), applied to creatures in the sea in Revelation's judgment scenes and to Daniel's beast imagery.","core_relation":"NO_CONSENSUS","extension_relation":"DIFFERENT_REFERENT","boundary_disagreement":"The book does not engage the passages the consensus treats as central (Ezekiel 1/10, Revelation 4-5); it instead targets a different set of occurrences (Rev 8:9; 16:3; Dan 7) and assigns a geopolitical referent (nations) that no consensus response or listed alternative mentions. If the book intended its definition to cover the four throne creatures as well, that would harden into contradiction, but its printed citations point away from the throne visions.","material_contradiction":"None demonstrated within the same context: the consensus identification (cherubim around the throne) concerns Ezekiel 1/10 and Revelation 4-5, while the book's identification (nations) is anchored to sea creatures in Revelation 8:9 and 16:3 and Daniel's beast symbolism. The two claims address different textual occurrences of the phrase, so the book's reading is absent from consensus rather than a replacement of it — though it would contradict the angelic identification if extended to the throne visions.","rationale":"The book's core identification — living creature as a nation/organized people, the counterpart of the symbolic beast — appears in none of the four blind responses, neither as primary meaning nor as any alternative (angelic cherubim, Evangelists, Christ's attributes, all creation, tribal standards, zodiac, or plain animate beings). Moreover, the book's proof-texts (Dan 7:3,17; Rev 8:9; 16:3) are entirely disjoint from the consensus proof-texts (Ezek 1/10; Rev 4-5), indicating the book is interpreting different occurrences of the term rather than contradicting the consensus on the same occurrences. This is absence from consensus, not head-on contradiction of the same referent, so NOVEL fits better than DIVERGENT.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT: the glossary term is 'Living creature' simpliciter, and any reader would apply the book's definition to the famous living creatures of Revelation 4 and Ezekiel 1, where 'nations' flatly contradicts the settled cherubim identification. Additionally, the printed citations only weakly support the book's own claim — Daniel 7 establishes beast = king/kingdom, but no cited verse explicitly equates 'living creature' with a nation; Rev 8:9 and 16:3 require the further unstated premise that 'sea' means peoples.","confidence":"medium"}
